title: Git — Deep Dive (Pro Git Book Coverage)
description: Git internals (objects, refs, DAG), rebase/merge, bisect, stash, hooks, cherry-pick, workflows (GitFlow, trunk-based, squash merge), conflict resolution, monorepo, LFS. Covers the full Pro Git book as listed by Turing.

questions.prompt: Git stores data as a content-addressed object store. The four object types are:
options: commit, tree, blob, tag
commit, branch, blob, ref
commit, file, directory, snapshot
push, pull, merge, rebase
questions.explanation: Git's object database stores: blob (file content), tree (directory listing of blobs/trees + filenames), commit (snapshot = pointer to root tree + parent commits + metadata), and tag (annotated tag object pointing to a commit). All are content-addressed by SHA-1/SHA-256.

questions.prompt: `git cat-file -t abc1234` returns 'blob'. This means abc1234 is:
options: A commit object
The raw content of a file stored in Git's object DB
A reference to a branch
A tag object
questions.explanation: Blob objects store raw file contents — no filename, no metadata. The filename is in the tree object that references this blob. Two files with identical content share one blob (content deduplication is automatic in Git).

questions.prompt: In Git, `HEAD` is:
options: Always a SHA pointing to the latest commit
A symbolic ref pointing to the currently checked-out branch (or detached to a commit SHA)
The first commit in the repository
A special branch that can't be deleted
questions.explanation: `HEAD` usually points to the current branch ref (e.g., `ref: refs/heads/main`). When you `git checkout abc1234`, HEAD becomes 'detached' — pointing directly to a SHA. `git branch` shows which branch HEAD tracks.

questions.prompt: What does `git gc` do and when is it needed?
options: Garbage-collects unreachable objects (orphaned commits, blobs) and repacks loose objects into packfiles for efficiency
Removes all untracked files from the working tree
Cleans the local cache of remote branches
Resets the index to match HEAD
questions.explanation: `git gc` (garbage collect): removes objects not reachable from any ref (orphaned by force-push, rebase, etc.) and packs loose objects. Run automatically by Git over time. Useful after aggressive history rewriting to reclaim disk space.

questions.prompt: Difference between `git merge` (non-fast-forward) and `git rebase`:
options: Merge creates a merge commit preserving history topology; rebase rewrites commits onto the target branch tip, creating a linear history
Rebase is always safer for shared branches; merge is for local branches only
Merge rewrites history; rebase preserves it
They produce identical results in all cases
questions.explanation: Merge: preserves full history including branch topology with a merge commit (good for audit trails). Rebase: replays commits on top of the target, creating new SHAs and linear history (cleaner log, but rewrites history — NEVER rebase shared public branches).

questions.prompt: Why should you NEVER `git push --force` to a shared branch like `main`?
options: It deletes the branch
It rewrites the remote's history — teammates who have already fetched the old history now have diverged refs and must force-pull or reset, potentially losing work
It requires admin permissions and fails silently
Force push is fine; you just need to notify teammates
questions.explanation: Force push overwrites the remote ref. Anyone who fetched before the rewrite now has commits that no longer exist on remote — their local branch has diverged. They must `git reset --hard origin/main` or lose unpushed work. Prefer `--force-with-lease` which fails if the remote changed since your last fetch.

questions.prompt: `git rebase -i HEAD~3` lets you:
options: Merge the last 3 commits into main
Interactively rewrite the last 3 commits: reorder, squash, fixup, edit, or drop them
Revert the last 3 commits
Cherry-pick 3 commits from another branch
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase opens an editor with the last 3 commits. Commands: `pick` (keep), `squash`/`s` (combine with previous commit), `fixup`/`f` (squash but discard this message), `edit`/`e` (pause to amend), `drop`/`d` (remove commit), `reword`/`r` (change message).

questions.prompt: After `git rebase -i` you have a conflict. To continue after resolving:
options: `git rebase --continue` after staging resolved files
`git rebase --skip` always
`git commit` then `git rebase --continue`
`git merge --continue`
questions.explanation: Resolve conflicts in the editor, `git add` the resolved files (don't commit), then `git rebase --continue`. Git replays the next commit. `--skip` skips the conflicting commit entirely. `--abort` cancels the whole rebase and returns to the pre-rebase state.

questions.prompt: `git cherry-pick abc123` does what?
options: Merges the branch containing abc123
Applies the diff introduced by commit abc123 onto the current branch as a new commit (new SHA, same changes)
Reverts commit abc123
Moves abc123 to the current branch, removing it from its original branch
questions.explanation: Cherry-pick copies the *changes* from a specific commit (the diff of parent → commit) and applies them as a new commit on the current branch. The new commit has a different SHA. Original commit is untouched. Useful for backporting hotfixes to release branches.

questions.prompt: `git bisect` is used to:
options: Split a large commit into smaller commits
Binary search through commit history to find the first commit that introduced a bug
Compare two branches for differences
Merge two divergent branches with conflict detection
questions.explanation: Workflow: `git bisect start`, mark a bad commit (`git bisect bad`) and a known-good commit (`git bisect good SHA`). Git checks out the midpoint. You test, mark good/bad, repeat. Git binary-searches to find the first bad commit in O(log n) steps.

questions.prompt: You have 1000 commits to search with `git bisect`. Maximum number of test steps needed:
options: ~31 (log₂ of log₂ 1000)
questions.explanation: Binary search: each step halves the search space. log₂(1000) ≈ 10. Compare to linear search which would require up to 1000 steps. Git bisect shows you: 'Bisecting: 499 revisions left to test after this (roughly 9 steps)'.

questions.prompt: `git stash` saves uncommitted changes. `git stash pop` vs `git stash apply` differ in:
options: `pop` removes the stash after applying; `apply` keeps the stash in the stash list
`pop` applies to a new branch; `apply` applies to current branch
`apply` is only for staged changes; `pop` handles all changes
They are identical
questions.explanation: `git stash pop` = apply + drop (remove from stash list). `git stash apply stash@{0}` applies but keeps the stash entry, so you can apply it to multiple branches. Use `git stash list` to see all stashes; `git stash drop` to manually remove.

questions.prompt: To stash untracked new files as well as modified tracked files:
options: `git stash`
`git stash -u` or `git stash --include-untracked`
`git stash --all`
`git stash --new`
questions.explanation: `git stash` only stashes changes to tracked files. `-u` (--include-untracked) also stashes new untracked files. `--all` includes ignored files too. Know this because missing new files in a stash is a common surprise.

questions.prompt: `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, `--mixed HEAD~1`, and `--hard HEAD~1` differ in what they do to the working tree and staging area:
options: soft: moves HEAD only (staged changes preserved, working tree untouched); mixed: moves HEAD + clears staging (changes in working tree); hard: moves HEAD + clears staging + discards working tree changes
hard: moves HEAD only; mixed: clears staging; soft: discards everything
All three do the same thing to history; difference is only in speed
soft and mixed are identical; hard also deletes the commit from history
questions.explanation: soft = HEAD moves, index (stage) unchanged → changes still staged. mixed = HEAD moves, index reset to HEAD → changes appear as unstaged modifications. hard = HEAD moves, index reset, working tree reset → changes GONE (destructive). All three rewrite history — never use on shared branches.

questions.prompt: `git reflog` is your safety net because:
options: It backs up your repository to a remote server
It records every position HEAD has pointed to, allowing recovery of commits after reset --hard, rebase, or accidental branch deletion
It shows the diff of every commit
It logs all `git push` operations
questions.explanation: Reflog keeps a local history of all ref updates (HEAD moves) for 90 days. After `git reset --hard` or a bad rebase, `git reflog` shows previous SHAs. `git checkout -b recovery SHA` restores the lost state. The reflog is purely local — not shared.

questions.prompt: Git hooks are stored in `.git/hooks/`. Which hook prevents a commit if tests fail?
options: pre-receive
pre-commit
commit-msg
post-commit
questions.explanation: `pre-commit` runs before the commit message editor opens. If it exits non-zero, the commit is aborted. Used for: running linters, type-check, tests. `commit-msg` validates the commit message format. `pre-push` runs before pushing. `post-commit` runs after — for notifications, cannot cancel.

questions.prompt: Husky is a popular npm package for Git hooks. It works by:
options: Modifying `.git/hooks/` scripts to invoke npm scripts defined in package.json
Running hooks inside Docker containers
Replacing Git's hook system with a separate daemon
Only working with GitHub Actions — not local hooks
questions.explanation: Husky sets up `.git/hooks/pre-commit` (etc.) to call `npx husky` which then runs the scripts configured in package.json or `.husky/` directory. Combined with lint-staged (runs linters only on staged files), it's the standard setup for JS/TS projects.

questions.prompt: GitFlow defines these long-lived branches:
options: main and develop, with feature/, release/, and hotfix/ short-lived branches off them
main only, with feature branches off it
main, staging, and develop as permanent branches
One branch per environment (dev, qa, staging, prod)
questions.explanation: GitFlow: `main` (production), `develop` (integration). Feature branches from develop; merged back to develop. Release branches from develop; merged to both main and develop. Hotfix branches from main; merged to both main and develop. Heavy process — less popular now vs trunk-based.

questions.prompt: Trunk-based development (TBD) recommendation for teams over 4 developers is:
options: All developers commit directly to main, multiple times per day
Short-lived feature branches (< 2 days) merged via PR to main; feature flags gate incomplete features
Long-lived feature branches with monthly merges
Each developer has a personal long-lived branch
questions.explanation: TBD: branches are short-lived (1–2 days max) to avoid merge hell. Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, etc.) decouple deployment from release — code can be in production but hidden. Enables CI/CD: every push to main is deployable. Contrast with GitFlow's heavy release process.

questions.prompt: Squash merge on a PR: you merge 12 commits from a feature branch into main as one commit. Trade-off:
options: Pro: clean linear history on main, easier to revert the entire feature; Con: loses granular commit history from the branch
Pro: preserves all 12 commits on main; Con: requires force push
Pro: faster than regular merge; Con: creates merge conflicts
No trade-off — squash is always better than merge commit
questions.explanation: Squash merge: main stays clean with one logical commit per feature (easy to `git revert` the whole feature). Trade-off: `git blame` on main only shows the squash commit, not which of the 12 sub-commits introduced each line. GitHub/GitLab offer this as a PR merge strategy.

questions.prompt: A merge conflict appears when:
options: Two branches added the same file
Two branches modified the same lines of the same file in incompatible ways (or one branch deleted a file the other modified)
A branch is more than 100 commits behind main
The file size exceeds Git's limit
questions.explanation: Git auto-merges changes to different lines. Conflicts occur when: same lines changed differently on both sides, or one side deleted a file the other modified. Git marks conflicts with `<<<<<<< HEAD`, `=======`, `>>>>>>> branch`. Three-way merge uses the common ancestor to understand each side's intent.

questions.prompt: `git merge -X ours` resolves all conflicts by:
options: Keeping only your branch's changes on conflicts
Keeping only the incoming branch's changes on conflicts
Interactively prompting for each conflict
Using a 3-way merge algorithm
questions.explanation: `-X ours` (ours strategy eXtension): on conflict, automatically take the current branch's version. `-X theirs` takes the incoming branch's version. These are dangerous — they silently discard the other side. Use only when you're certain one side's changes are correct (e.g., generated files).

questions.prompt: Git submodules: a project that includes another Git repository as a subdirectory. The parent repo stores:
options: A copy of the submodule's files at the time of addition
A pointer (SHA) to a specific commit in the submodule's repository, not the files themselves
A symlink to the submodule's local path
The submodule's latest main branch always
questions.explanation: Submodules store a reference: which repo URL + which commit SHA. `git clone --recurse-submodules` clones the parent AND checks out the pinned commit of each submodule. The submodule is NOT automatically updated — you explicitly update to a new commit and commit that pointer change.

questions.prompt: Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces large binary files in the repo with:
options: Compressed zlib streams
Pointer files containing the file's SHA and size; actual content stored on a separate LFS server
Base64-encoded file contents in commits
Delta-compressed binary patches
questions.explanation: Git LFS: tracked files (e.g., `*.psd`, `*.mp4`) are replaced with text pointer files in commits. Actual binary content is uploaded to an LFS server (GitHub/GitLab host one). During checkout, Git LFS downloads the real files. Keeps repo size small; large files don't slow clone.

questions.prompt: `git blame -L 42,55 src/api.ts` shows:
options: Who changed lines 42–55, in which commit, and when
All commits that touched the file between dates 42 and 55
The diff of lines 42–55 between two commits
The merge history of lines 42–55
questions.explanation: `git blame` annotates each line with: commit SHA, author, date, and original line number. `-L 42,55` limits to lines 42–55. Useful for tracking when a specific line was introduced. Follow renames: `git blame --follow -C` detects code moved from other files.

questions.prompt: `git branch -d feature/login` vs `git branch -D feature/login`:
options: -d deletes only if branch is fully merged into current branch; -D force-deletes regardless
-D deletes from remote; -d deletes locally
-d is for detached HEAD branches; -D is for normal branches
They are identical
questions.explanation: `-d` (safe delete): refuses to delete if the branch has unmerged commits — Git protects you from losing work. `-D` force deletes even with unmerged commits. Always prefer `-d`; use `-D` only when you're certain you don't need the branch (e.g., after squash-merging via PR).

questions.prompt: Lightweight tags vs annotated tags (`git tag -a v1.0 -m 'release'`) in Git:
options: Lightweight: just a pointer (ref) to a commit; Annotated: full Git object with tagger, date, message — can be signed with GPG
Annotated tags are deleted on push; lightweight are permanent
Lightweight tags are pushed automatically; annotated require --tags flag
They behave identically — just different syntax
questions.explanation: Lightweight tags = a named ref to a commit SHA (like a branch that doesn't move). Annotated tags are first-class Git objects with full metadata and can be GPG-signed for verification. Best practice: use annotated tags for releases; lightweight for temporary local markers.

questions.prompt: In a monorepo (all services in one Git repo), `git sparse-checkout` helps by:
options: Preventing all developers from seeing other services' code
Checking out only a subset of directories — developers only download the parts of the repo they work on
Combining multiple repos into one
Running Git operations only on changed files
questions.explanation: Sparse checkout: define which paths to materialise in the working tree. A backend dev working on `/services/api` doesn't need `/services/mobile` on disk. Critical for large monorepos (Google/Meta scale) where the full tree would be gigabytes. Combined with partial clone (`--filter=blob:none`) for fast initial clones.

questions.prompt: `git fetch` vs `git pull` difference:
options: fetch downloads all remote objects and updates remote-tracking refs but does NOT change the working branch; pull = fetch + merge (or rebase) into the current branch
fetch only lists what's new; pull downloads
They are identical — just aliases
pull is safer than fetch because it shows a diff before merging
questions.explanation: `fetch` is always safe: updates `origin/main` (remote-tracking ref) without touching your local `main`. You review changes before merging. `pull` = `fetch` + `merge` (or `--rebase`), which immediately changes your local branch. Best practice: `git fetch` then inspect, then `git merge origin/main`.

questions.prompt: Conventional Commits format (`feat:`, `fix:`, `chore:`, `BREAKING CHANGE:`) enables:
options: Automatic semantic version bumping and CHANGELOG generation by tooling that reads commit types
Enforced code review workflows
Automatic PR creation for each commit
Faster git log performance
questions.explanation: Conventional Commits is a specification for commit messages. Tools like `semantic-release` or `release-please` read commit types: `fix:` → patch bump, `feat:` → minor bump, `BREAKING CHANGE:` → major bump. Enables fully automated versioning and changelog generation in CI.

questions.prompt: When rebasing and you have conflicts in 5 consecutive commits, you must:
options: Resolve all 5 at once
Resolve each conflict one-by-one as rebase replays each commit — git stops after each conflicting commit
Abort and use merge instead
Use --skip to skip all conflicting commits
questions.explanation: Interactive rebase replays commits one at a time. If commit 3 conflicts, Git stops. You resolve, `git add`, `git rebase --continue`. Then commit 4 may conflict — you resolve again. This is why rebasing many old commits onto a branch with lots of divergence can be painful — each commit may conflict.

questions.prompt: `git log --oneline --graph --all` shows:
options: Only the current branch's history
A visual ASCII-art DAG of all branches' commit histories in the terminal
All commits by a specific author
The diff of each commit
questions.explanation: `--graph` draws branch/merge topology as ASCII. `--all` includes all branches and tags (not just current). `--oneline` condenses each commit to one line (SHA + message). This is the quickest way to visualise the full repository topology.

questions.prompt: The `pre-push` hook is useful for:
options: Preventing pushes if integration tests fail — more thorough than pre-commit but runs just before pushing to remote
Formatting commit messages before push
Auto-rebasing before pushing
Checking remote permissions
questions.explanation: `pre-push` receives the remote name and URL. It can run heavier checks (integration tests, build) that are too slow for `pre-commit`. If it exits non-zero, the push is aborted. Trade-off: slower push workflow, but catches issues before they reach CI.

questions.prompt: A teammate force-pushed to `main` and teammates now have diverged history. Walk through the steps to recover without losing anyone's work.

rubric.criterion: Immediate action: coordinate with team — freeze all pushes
Use git reflog to find the pre-force-push SHA
Each affected dev identifies their unpushed commits (git log origin/main..HEAD)
Cherry-pick or rebase unpushed commits onto updated main
Prevention: use --force-with-lease and protect main on GitHub/GitLab

questions.prompt: Explain what happens under the hood when you run `git commit -m 'fix: null check'`. Describe each Git object created and how HEAD is updated.

rubric.criterion: Staged files become blob objects in the object store (content-addressed by SHA)
A tree object is created representing the directory with updated blob references
A commit object is created pointing to the root tree, parent commit SHA, and containing author/committer/message
HEAD (or the branch it points to) is updated to point to the new commit SHA
Explains SHA is a content hash — identical content = same SHA, enabling deduplication
